texts.label: text
texts.orig: A dragon guards the entrance to the Watts Chapel. Its image is carved into an enormous set of oak doors, where tangled limbs and a menacing grin are pierced by an iron cross. Above, a grand arch features angelic faces that alternate between looking up in hope and down in sorrow. This miracle in terracotta stretches across the exterior of the building, where ancient symbols of hope, liberty and spirituality adorn buttresses, capitals and columns.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: This glorious entryway is just a foretaste of the treasures that await inside. The glittering interior is an ode to heaven and earth, as richly decorated as the pages of an illuminated manuscript. Crimson-covered seraphs and cherubic faces stretch into the curves of a magnificent dome, while below, angels clutch discs that depict the duality of human existence, all of which are knotted together among the blooming vines of a Tree of Life.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: This astonishing Arts and Crafts building was the brainchild of Mary Watts, wife of Symbolist artist George Frederic Watts. After the couple moved into their new Surrey home of Limnerslease in 1891, she soon went about conceiving a place of spiritual contemplation for their local community, specifically a mortuary chapel, where loved ones could attend to the dead before burial.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Mary Watts was no stranger to painting or sculpture, having trained at the Slade School of Fine Art. There her deft ability with clay had been evident, yet the chapel offered her the opportunity to flex her creative muscles as never before. She set about manifesting the signs of ancient spiritual languages - from Egyptian hieroglyphs to Celtic crosses - into a single, spectacular space. In a 1905 essay explaining the nuances of these complex decorations, she writes: 'A symbol may well be compared to a magic key. In one hand it is nothing more than a piece of quaintly wrought iron, in another it unlocks a door into a world of enchantment.'

There her deft ability with clay had been evident, yet the chapel offered her the opportunity to flex her creative muscles as never before. In one hand it is nothing more than a piece of quaintly wrought iron, in another it unlocks a door into a world of enchantment.'

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Contemporary sculptor Halima Cassell remembers the first time she experienced this world, visiting the chapel in preparation for an exhibition at the Wattses' purpose-built art gallery. 'It was truly astonishing,' she says. 'I have always been interested in religious buildings, but this was the first time I felt an overwhelming sense of femininity and warmth. Mary Watts's use of pattern, craftsmanship and inclusion of symbolism from different cultures gives the building an incredible sense of harmony.' Your World of Interiors

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Cassell was pleasantly surprised to find so many affinities with an artist who had been working over a hundred years ago. Like Watts, her beautifully crafted pieces balance architectural geometry with sweeping organic lines, and a shared interest in the commonality of spiritual existence is visualised through motifs of love and eternity. These include the Bodhi leaf and the Sacred Heart, as well as celebrations of humanity's virtues. In fact, Cassell's ongoing series titled 'Virtues of Unity' sees her collecting clay from different corners of the world and carving vessels that symbolise ideas such as honour, felicity, valour and more. She created four new pieces for this exhibition, which are named after the specific virtues that decorate the chapel interior. Your World of Interiors

texts.orig: In addition, a new sculpture called Bo Orb formed from clay taken from the very stream that Watts would have used, one happily unearthed by the head gardener. The acute, interlocking lines of this curvaceous form evoke the same sensuality that dominates the chapel, as well as nods to the presence of light and dark in all things.
